label: Person
name: Lucius Aemilius Regillus
summary:
Lucius Aemilius Regillus, a Roman praetor and admiral, achieved critical naval victories for the Roman Republic during the pivotal Roman-Syrian War (192–188 BCE). His command of the Roman fleet in the Aegean Sea was instrumental in neutralizing the formidable naval power of Antiochus III the Great, thereby securing Roman control over vital maritime routes and facilitating the eventual land victory. Regillus's strategic successes cemented Rome's burgeoning influence in the Hellenistic East, marking a significant step in its transition from a regional Italian power to a dominant Mediterranean hegemon.

Regillus's defining moment arrived in 190 BCE at the Battle of Myonessus, off the coast of Ionia. Leading a fleet of 58 Roman and 25 Rhodian ships, he decisively engaged a larger Seleucid fleet of 89 vessels under the command of Polyxenidas. Utilizing superior tactics, including the Rhodian ships' maneuverability and the Romans' grappling hooks, Regillus inflicted a crushing defeat on Antiochus's navy, sinking or capturing 42 Seleucid ships while losing only two of his own. This victory, following earlier skirmishes and blockades, effectively crippled the Seleucid naval capacity, denying Antiochus the ability to reinforce his armies in Greece and Asia Minor by sea.

The Battle of Myonessus, under Regillus's command, had profound and immediate consequences. It ensured Roman naval supremacy in the Aegean, paving the way for the Scipios' land invasion of Asia Minor and culminating in the decisive Battle of Magnesia in 189 BCE. Regillus's triumph contributed directly to the Treaty of Apamea (188 BCE), which severely curtailed Seleucid power, stripped Antiochus of his territories in Asia Minor, and firmly established Rome as the arbiter of the Hellenistic world. His actions underscored the vital role of naval power in Roman expansion and secured the Republic's strategic advantage for decades to come.
